newsitem.title: USA: Stocks, bonds fall on rate worries, dollar mixed.
newsitem.headline: Stocks, bonds fall on rate worries, dollar mixed.

text.p: Stocks fell Wednesday in an intensified sell-off of technology shares, and bonds also moved lower.
The dollar was mixed against major currencies.
In commodities markets, oil prices rose on forecasts of colder weather in the Northeast, the world's largest market for heating oil.

The Dow Jones industrial average lost 45.79 points to 7,039.37, after falling more than 70 points earlier. The drop ended a string of two record closing highs of 7,085.16 on Tuesday and 7,079.39 on Monday.
In the broader market, losers beat winners 1,566 to 934 on heavy volume of 483.1 million on the New York Stock Exchange.
The broad sell-off took the Standard & Poor's index of 500 stocks and Nasdaq Composite indexes down by nearly one full percent.
Beyond the technology sector, the stiffest selling seemed directed toward financial and pharmaceutical stocks, which have posted the sharpest rallies this year.
During the latest gains by the Dow, investors were clearly unwilling to broaden stock picks beyond mainly defensive blue-chip issues, undermining the large-cap rally, analysts said.
"Bull markets don't scream ahead when defensive names are in the leadership," said Scott Bleier, chief investment strategist at Prime Charter Ltd.
"With the market as fragmented as it is, we'll have very significant problems making headway and be subjected to substantial profit-taking at the high end of our trading range," he said.
The bond market remained nervous about inflation even though a closely watched Federal Reserve report released Wednesday showed price pressures were under control.
The 30-year Treasury bond fell 11/32, or $3.44 on a $1,000 bond, which raised its yield to 6.88 percent from 6.85 percent at Tuesday's close. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.

In its Beige Book report on U.S. economic conditions, the Fed described price pressures as "temperate." Likewise, wage gains remain moderate and show no signs of spiking higher despite tight labour markets, it said.
The news temporarily cheered financial markets, triggering a brief recovery in both stocks and bonds. But the sense of caution that has gripped the market of late quickly returned.

"I didn't see anything, frankly, that would be a smoking gun for a tightening by the Fed," said Peter Canelo, chief investment strategist at Dean Witter. "But I think everyone on the planet knows they're going to tighten (raise rates) and it's just a question of when and by how much."
For now, analysts said, the interest rate issue offers a welcome opportunity to cash in on some of the latest gains for blue chips.

In currency markets, the dollar fell against the German mark after Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer again objected to strength in the U.S. currency. But the dollar rose against the yen as Japanese interest rates fell.

In late trading, the dollar fetched 1.6928 marks, down from 1.7037 marks late on Tuesday. The dollar rose to 122.27 yen from 121.78 yen as the yield on the benchmark 10-year Japanese government bond fell to a record low of 2.295 percent.

At the New York Mercantile Exchange, oil prices closed higher as forecasts for colder weather in the Northeast overshadowed U.S. oil inventory data which showed higher-than-expected stocks of crude oil.
April crude oil closed up 51 cents a barrel at $20.62, with April heating oil up 1.25 cents a gallon at 54.08 cents and April gasoline up 0.77 cent a gallon at 64.63 cents.
Overseas, London's FTSE 100 share index settled 21.8 points lower at 4,422.5, near the day's worst levels at 4,419.2. In Tokyo, the Nikkei 225 average closed down 85.45 points at 18,183.27.
